config.title: FastAPI

intro.title: FastAPI
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple web API using FastAPI, a modern Python framework for creating APIs quickly. You'll learn the core concept of defining endpoints that handle HTTP requests and return JSON responses. The main technologies involved include FastAPI itself, Pydantic for data validation, and Uvicorn as the ASGI server to run your application. By the end, you'll have a working API that can receive requests and send back structured data, giving you a foundational understanding of how web APIs are built with Python.
intro.usecase: FastAPI powers modern web APIs that serve as backends for applications like e-commerce platforms, where it handles product searches, user authentication, and payment processing. Developers use it to build real-time dashboards that display analytics data, or to create RESTful APIs for mobile apps that submit forms and fetch dynamic content. In enterprise settings, FastAPI is used for internal tools like admin panels that manage user permissions and data filters, enabling efficient CRUD operations and secure data exchanges.

objectives: Implement a basic FastAPI application with a root endpoint
Configure route handlers to respond to HTTP GET requests
Construct API endpoints with path parameters to handle dynamic data
Apply Pydantic models to validate and structure request/response data
Initialize and integrate a Uvicorn server to run the FastAPI application
Manipulate response data to return JSON-formatted content
Bind query parameters to endpoint functions for filtering requests

steps.title: Import FastAPI and create the app instance
steps.instruction: Import FastAPI from the fastapi module and create an instance of the FastAPI class named app.
steps.hint: Use the 'from ... import ...' syntax to import FastAPI, then instantiate it with app = FastAPI().
steps.analogousExample:
# Importing a class and creating an instance
from datetime import datetime
now = datetime.now()
steps.seedCode: # Import FastAPI and create the app instance here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the FastAPI module imported and an app instance ready to define routes.
successCriteria: FastAPI is imported from 'fastapi' and an instance named 'app' is created.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've imported FastAPI and created an instance named 'app'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've imported FastAPI from 'fastapi' and created an instance named 'app'.

steps.title: Define your first route with a GET endpoint
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'read_root' and decorate it with '@app.get("/")' to define a GET endpoint that returns a simple welcome message.
steps.hint: Use the @app.get decorator above your function definition. The function should return a string like 'Welcome to FastAPI!'.
steps.seedCode:
# Import FastAPI and create the app instance here
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

# Define your first GET endpoint here
steps.expectedOutcome: A GET endpoint at the root path ('/') that returns a welcome message when accessed.
successCriteria: The function 'read_root' is defined and decorated with '@app.get("/")', and returns a string message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have both the decorator '@app.get("/")' and a function that returns a string.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a function with the @app.get("/") decorator above it that returns a welcome message.

steps.title: Add a path parameter to the route
steps.instruction: Create a new GET endpoint at the path '/items/{item_id}' that returns a JSON response containing the item_id captured from the URL path parameter.
steps.hint: Use the @app.get decorator with the path containing curly braces around 'item_id'. Define a function that takes 'item_id' as a parameter and returns a dictionary like {'item_id': item_id}.
steps.seedCode:
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

# Define your first GET endpoint here

# Create a new GET endpoint at /items/{item_id} that returns the item_id from the path parameter
steps.expectedOutcome: A new route is added that dynamically captures 'item_id' from the URL and returns it in a JSON response.
successCriteria: The code includes a GET endpoint at '/items/{item_id}' with a function that accepts 'item_id' as a parameter and returns a dictionary containing the item_id.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have the @app.get decorator with the correct path pattern '/items/{item_id}' and a function that returns a dictionary with the item_id.
steps.feedbackWrong: The endpoint isn't quite right. Remember to use @app.get('/items/{item_id}') and define a function that takes 'item_id' as a parameter and returns {'item_id': item_id}.

steps.title: Add query parameters to the endpoint
steps.instruction: Modify the existing GET endpoint at /items/{item_id} to accept an optional query parameter named 'q' with a default value of None.
steps.hint: Add a function parameter 'q' to your endpoint function and give it a default value like 'q: str = None'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The endpoint will accept requests like GET /items/5?q=fastapi and include the query parameter in the response.
successCriteria: The endpoint function has an optional parameter 'q' with a default value of None.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you added 'q' as a parameter with a default value like 'q: str = None'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The endpoint doesn't have an optional query parameter. Add 'q' as a parameter with a default value.

steps.title: Create a POST endpoint to add data
steps.instruction: Create a new POST endpoint at the path '/items/' that accepts JSON data in the request body and returns the received data.
steps.hint: Use the @app.post decorator above a function that takes a parameter with a type hint. The function should return the data.
steps.expectedOutcome: A POST endpoint is defined at '/items/' that will accept JSON request data and echo it back in the response.
successCriteria: A POST endpoint is defined at '/items/' using @app.post, with a function that takes a parameter (e.g., 'item') and returns it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using @app.post('/items/') and defining a function that takes a parameter (like 'item') and returns it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The POST endpoint isn't correctly defined. You need to use @app.post('/items/') and create a function that accepts and returns data.

steps.title: Define a Pydantic model for request validation
steps.instruction: Import BaseModel from pydantic and define an Item model with name (str) and price (float) fields.
steps.hint: Use 'from pydantic import BaseModel' and create a class that inherits from BaseModel with the required fields.
steps.analogousExample:
# Similar: define a Pydantic model
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Product(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have a Pydantic model named Item with name and price fields, ready to be used for request validation.
successCriteria: BaseModel is imported from pydantic and an Item model with name:str and price:float fields is defined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've imported BaseModel from pydantic and defined the Item class with both name (str) and price (float) fields.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Item model isn't defined correctly. Check that you've imported BaseModel and created a class with the required fields and type hints.

steps.title: Add a PUT endpoint to update data
steps.instruction: Create a PUT endpoint at '/items/{item_id}' that accepts an Item model in the request body and returns the updated item with its ID.
steps.hint: Use the @app.put decorator with the path '/items/{item_id}'. The function should take item_id as a path parameter and an Item instance as a request body parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: A PUT endpoint is added to update items by their ID, using the Item model for request validation.
successCriteria: The PUT endpoint is defined with the correct path and decorator, accepts both item_id and an Item instance, and returns a dictionary with both values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your endpoint uses @app.put, has the correct path '/items/{item_id}', and accepts both item_id and an Item parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PUT endpoint is missing or incorrect. Review the path, decorator, and parameters needed.

steps.title: Add a DELETE endpoint to remove data
steps.instruction: Create a DELETE endpoint at '/items/{item_id}' that returns a confirmation message when an item is deleted. Use the @app.delete decorator and define a function that takes the item_id path parameter.
steps.hint: Follow the pattern of the previous endpoints: use a decorator with the path, define a function with the parameter, and return a dictionary with a confirmation message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The DELETE endpoint is defined and returns a JSON response with a confirmation message when an item is deleted.
successCriteria: A DELETE endpoint is created at '/items/{item_id}' using @app.delete decorator, with a function that takes item_id as a path parameter and returns a dictionary containing a confirmation message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct decorator (@app.delete) and returning a dictionary with a confirmation message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The DELETE endpoint is not correctly implemented. Check that you're using @app.delete('/items/{item_id}') and returning a dictionary like {'message': 'Item deleted'}.

steps.title: Run the FastAPI application with Uvicorn
steps.instruction: At the bottom of your file, add a conditional block that runs the FastAPI app with Uvicorn when the script is executed directly.
steps.hint: Use the standard Python idiom: if __name__ == '__main__': then call uvicorn.run(app, host='0.0.0.0', port=8000).
steps.analogousExample:
# Similar: running a FastAPI app
if __name__ == '__main__':
    import uvicorn
    uvicorn.run(app, host='0.0.0.0', port=8000)
steps.expectedOutcome: The API will be ready to start with a development server when you run the script directly.
successCriteria: The conditional block with if __name__ == '__main__': is added, and uvicorn.run(app, host='0.0.0.0', port=8000) is called inside it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a conditional block, but it may not be complete. Make sure to import uvicorn inside the block and call uvicorn.run with the app instance, host, and port.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional block to run the app with Uvicorn is missing or incorrect. Please add the standard Python idiom to start the development server.

steps.title: Test the API endpoints
steps.instruction: Run the application with Uvicorn and test each endpoint (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to ensure they return the expected responses.
steps.hint: Add the conditional block at the bottom of your file to run the app when the script is executed directly.
steps.analogousExample:
# Running a FastAPI app with Uvicorn
if __name__ == '__main__':
    import uvicorn
    uvicorn.run(app, host='0.0.0.0', port=8000)
steps.expectedOutcome: The application will start and be ready to handle requests at http://localhost:8000. You can test each endpoint using a tool like curl, Postman, or your browser.
successCriteria: The conditional block to run the app with Uvicorn is added and the application can be started.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to include the conditional block with `if __name__ == '__main__':` and the uvicorn.run() call.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the analogous example. You need to add the conditional block at the bottom of your file to run the app with Uvicorn.
